name: Hippocampus
func: A curved, seahorse-shaped structure deep in the medial temporal lobe. It turns new experiences into lasting memories of facts and events and builds a mental map for finding your way.

levels.kid:
Deep inside each side of your brain is a curly little part shaped like a **seahorse**. Its name, **hippocampus**, actually means "seahorse"!

The hippocampus is your **memory maker**. When something happens to you, like a fun birthday party, the hippocampus helps save it so you can remember it later.

It also helps you know where you are. When you remember the way to your friend's house, your hippocampus is drawing a map in your head.

Sleep helps your hippocampus do its job. While you sleep, it replays your day and helps store the important parts for a long time.
levels.hs:
The **hippocampus** is a curved ridge of gray matter in the **medial temporal lobe**. It forms the **floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle**, bulging into it. It runs from front to back along the inner edge of the temporal lobe, right above the **parahippocampal gyrus**, and curves up behind the thalamus. The **amygdala** sits just in front of its head. Its output fibers gather into the **fornix**, an arch-shaped tract that curves up and forward under the corpus callosum.

It has three parts: the wide **head** at the front, with bumps called digitations, the **body**, and the narrow **tail** at the back.

**What it does:**
- **Forms new declarative memories:** memories of facts and events you can consciously recall. It does not store them forever by itself; over time memories become more dependent on the cortex.
- **Spatial navigation:** it builds a "cognitive map" of your surroundings.
- It is not needed for learning skills like riding a bike or for short-term memory, like holding a number in mind for a few seconds.

The hippocampus is one of the few places where new neurons may continue to form in adults (in the **dentate gyrus**), though how much this happens in humans is debated. It is also very sensitive to low oxygen, seizures and long-term stress hormones.
levels.college:
**Hippocampal formation:** the **dentate gyrus**, the **hippocampus proper (cornu Ammonis, CA1–CA4)** and the **subiculum**, plus closely related entorhinal cortex. In cross-section these form two interlocking C-shapes. The hippocampus proper is **archicortex** (three-layered): stratum oriens, the **pyramidal layer**, and the stratum radiatum/lacunosum-moleculare. The dentate gyrus has a **granule cell layer**.

**Trisynaptic circuit:**
1. Entorhinal cortex layer II → **perforant path** → dentate granule cells.
2. Granule cells → **mossy fibers** → CA3 pyramidal cells.
3. CA3 → **Schaffer collaterals** → CA1 pyramidal cells.

CA3 also connects heavily to itself (recurrent collaterals). CA1 projects to the subiculum and back to entorhinal deep layers. A direct path from entorhinal layer III reaches CA1 (the **temporoammonic path**).

**Output:** the **alveus** on the ventricular surface collects axons into the **fimbria**, which becomes the **fornix**, projecting to the mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, septal nuclei and hypothalamus.

**Long axis:** the anterior (ventral in rodents) hippocampus is more linked to emotion and stress via the amygdala and hypothalamus; the posterior (dorsal in rodents) is more linked to precise spatial memory.

**Relations:** medially, the **choroidal fissure** separates it from the thalamus and contains the choroid plexus; above it is the temporal horn; the midbrain and PCA lie just medial to it.

**Blood supply:** **hippocampal arteries** from the **PCA** (and sometimes the anterior choroidal artery) supply it. CA1 (**Sommer's sector**) is especially vulnerable to low oxygen.
levels.phd:
**Long-term potentiation (LTP):** Bliss and Lømo (1973) showed that high-frequency stimulation of the perforant path produces a lasting increase in synaptic strength. At CA3-CA1 synapses, LTP requires **NMDA receptors**, which act as **coincidence detectors**: they open only when glutamate is bound *and* the postsynaptic membrane is depolarized, which removes the magnesium block. The resulting **calcium influx** activates **CaMKII**, which drives insertion of more **AMPA receptors**. Late LTP needs new gene expression and protein synthesis. Blocking NMDA receptors in the hippocampus impairs spatial learning in the **Morris water maze** (Morris 1986).

**Place cells:** O'Keefe and Dostrovsky (1971) found CA1/CA3 neurons that fire when a rat is in a particular location (Nobel Prize 2014 with the Mosers). Each environment gets its own set of active place cells (**remapping**). Other hippocampal cells encode time ("time cells") and social and conceptual information.

**Theta and sharp-wave ripples:** during exploration, place cells fire at progressively earlier phases of the **theta rhythm** (4–12 Hz) as an animal crosses a place field (**phase precession**), compressing sequences in time. During rest and slow-wave sleep, **sharp-wave ripples** (about 150–250 Hz) replay these sequences, often at high speed and sometimes in reverse. Disrupting ripples impairs memory consolidation (Girardeau and Buzsáki).

**Pattern separation and completion:** the dentate gyrus, with many sparsely active granule cells, is thought to make similar inputs more distinct (**pattern separation**), while the CA3 recurrent network can retrieve a whole memory from a partial cue (**pattern completion**).

**Consolidation theories:** standard consolidation theory says memories become hippocampus-independent over time; **multiple trace / trace transformation theory** says vivid episodic detail always requires the hippocampus.
levels.expert:
**The case of H.M.:** in 1953, Henry Molaison had both medial temporal lobes removed to treat severe epilepsy. Afterward he had profound **anterograde amnesia** (could not form new declarative memories) and some **retrograde amnesia**, yet his intelligence, short-term memory and **motor skill learning** (mirror drawing, studied by Brenda Milner) were preserved. This revealed that the hippocampus is essential for new declarative memory but not for skills.

**Conditions:**

- **Mesial temporal sclerosis (hippocampal sclerosis):** the commonest cause of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy. MRI: **hippocampal atrophy, increased T2/FLAIR signal and loss of internal architecture**. Neuron loss favors CA1 and CA4, with relative sparing of CA2.
- **Alzheimer disease:** hippocampal atrophy on MRI; memory tests show poor delayed recall not helped by cues.
- **Hypoxic-ischemic injury** (e.g., after cardiac arrest): selective CA1 loss causes amnesia.
- **Herpes simplex encephalitis:** asymmetric medial temporal inflammation; early antiviral treatment is critical.
- **Autoimmune limbic encephalitis** (e.g., LGI1 antibodies): memory loss, seizures (faciobrachial dystonic seizures), low blood sodium, and T2 hyperintense hippocampi; treated with immunotherapy.
- **Transient global amnesia:** sudden temporary anterograde amnesia lasting hours, with repetitive questioning; small DWI dots in CA1 may show up 24–72 h later. It resolves on its own.

**Bilateral** damage is needed for severe amnesia. Unilateral left hippocampal damage tends to affect verbal memory and right damage visual-spatial memory.

**Surgery:** for MTS, **anterior temporal lobectomy** or **selective amygdalohippocampectomy** yields high seizure-freedom rates. Before surgery, teams assess memory risk, sometimes with the **Wada test** (temporarily anesthetizing one hemisphere through a carotid catheter) or functional MRI. Less invasive options include **laser interstitial thermal therapy** and responsive neurostimulation for bilateral cases.

keyPoints: Medial temporal lobe; forms the floor of the temporal horn
Trisynaptic circuit: perforant path → mossy fibers → Schaffer collaterals
Needed for new declarative memory, not skills (patient H.M.)
CA1 is most vulnerable to low oxygen; MTS causes temporal lobe epilepsy

test.q: The hippocampus forms the floor of which part of the ventricular system?
choices: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle
test.explain: It bulges into the temporal (inferior) horn.

test.q: The axons of dentate granule cells that synapse on CA3 are called ______ fibers.
test.explain: Mossy fibers are the second step of the trisynaptic circuit.

test.q: Which receptor acts as a coincidence detector in hippocampal LTP?
test.explain: NMDA receptors need both glutamate and depolarization to open.

test.q: After surgery, patient H.M. could NOT:
choices: Form new memories of facts and events
Hold a number in short-term memory
test.explain: He had profound anterograde declarative amnesia but preserved skill learning.

test.q: Which CA region (Sommer's sector) is most vulnerable to low oxygen?
test.explain: CA1 pyramidal neurons die first after hypoxia-ischemia.

test.q: Hippocampal neurons that fire when an animal is in a specific location are:
test.explain: O'Keefe discovered place cells and shared the 2014 Nobel Prize.
